sound: small yo, which joins to the preceding sign and makes one mora with it
components: a small vertical turning into a lower loop
strokeOrder: draw the short upper horizontal from left to right
lift, begin above the horizontal, descend through it, then turn left and continue clockwise around the lower loop to the rightward finish
strokeOrderNote: Sirgazil's corrected 26-frame よ animation supplies the two-run order; KanjiVG's 03087 file holds the same two strokes in the same order for U+3087 itself, and Unicode names U+3087 HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL YO, so the movement is fitted to the smaller bundled glyph exactly as small ゅ is fitted from ゆ.

strokeOrderSource.citation: Sirgazil, Hiragana よ stroke order animation.gif, hiragana よ, 26 frames, 2.6 seconds (Wikimedia Commons, 1 October 2009; corrected first-stroke direction 4 January 2012); KanjiVG kanji/03087.svg, two stroke paths in the same order; the Unicode Standard names U+3087 HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL YO
strokeOrderSource.variation: The CC0 animation draws full-size よ in two pen-down runs with one lift: the short upper bar from left to right, then the stem descending through it and the clockwise lower loop. KanjiVG records U+3087 with the same two strokes in the same order. Unicode separately identifies U+3087 as small yo. This learner path therefore preserves the source's two-run movement while scaling and fitting it to the bundled Noto Sans JP small ょ outline; the cited animation demonstrates よ rather than a separately animated ょ, so the size adaptation is explicit rather than presented as independent handwriting evidence.

notes: A yōon sign: it fuses with the sign before it, so ち + ょ is one mora cho, as in ちょっと, a little. Its full-size twin よ takes a beat of its own, as in よろしく.
